headline: 9,500 pounds of lead azide. The Army blows it up.
summary: The Army plans to detonate 68 barrels of lead azide, 9,500 pounds, at its ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Wednesday. Staff found the barrels in March, crystallised and too unstable to move. The dust could carry lead 100 miles. Trump paused it Monday; then an appeals court lifted its stay and the Army said it is going ahead.
cover_answer: It can't be moved. A bump could set it off.
table_question: If every option is risky, who should get to decide?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In Iowa, the Army has 68 old barrels of explosive that got too touchy to move, so on Wednesday they will set it off on purpose, with everyone far away. It weighs about as much as three cars. People nearby will stay inside with the windows shut until the dust settles. The grown-ups have been planning it since March.
5-7.why: A planned bang is the anchor. On purpose, everyone far away, inside until it settles. Then stop.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes the loudest detail for the whole event, so the script makes the loud detail the plan: on purpose, with everyone far away. Three cars gives the weight a shape. Lead and brains can wait; a child this age reads your face before your words, so say it flat. Expect 'will it happen here?' No. One plant in Iowa.

8-12.script: In old barrels, lead azide grew crystals so touchy a bump could set them off, and cold makes it worse, so the Army blows up all 68 barrels Wednesday, before it freezes. The dust carries lead, a poison, so people nearby stay in and wash up after. Like ripping off a bandage: once, on your terms.
8-12.why: Barrels, crystals, cold, blast: a chain they can follow. Dust is the price.
8-12.why_long: An eight-year-old is building chains of cause and effect, and this one is all chain: barrels sat for decades, crystals grew, cold makes them touchier, so detonate before it freezes. The script hands over the chain, then the cost in lead dust, so the trade is theirs to judge. Expect 'why did they let it get so old?' Nobody has said.

13-17.script: Why blow it up instead of moving it? The Army says a bump could set off 9,500 pounds of crystallised lead azide, so a planned blast, dust and all, beats a surprise one. Second: Trump passed the call to a court and the governor-elect, who passed it back. Who owns it?
13-17.why: The blast is dangerous, and so is waiting. Let them weigh it.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once, and this story is two: a controlled blast spreads lead, and an uncontrolled one could come any day. The second pair is a president and a governor-elect each saying the other should decide. Give them both sides and let them argue. Expect 'who's right?' Nobody has shown a safe option.

5-7.a: Nobody is supposed to be anywhere near it. People close by stay inside until the dust settles.

8-12.a: It's a poison that hurts growing brains most. No amount is safe.

8-12.q: Why did it get so old?
8-12.a: Nobody has said. A senator wants an investigation.

13-17.a: The crystals are so touchy a bump could set them off. Moving is the risk.

13-17.q: Why pass it to a governor who isn't in office yet?
13-17.a: Trump didn't say. Rob Sand takes office January 12. He sent it back.
